part2.title: Describe an interesting conversation you had with a very old person
part2.answer: I'd like to describe a conversation I had with my grandfather when I was a child. It happened around Chinese New Year, when people in my hometown usually set off fireworks and firecrackers. I was actually quite scared of them because they were extremely loud, so I didn't want to join in. My grandfather noticed this and told me the traditional story of Nian, a fierce monster that was said to appear every winter and threaten villagers. According to the story, people eventually discovered that Nian was afraid of loud noises and fire, so they used firecrackers to drive it away. That's why setting off firecrackers became a traditional part of Chinese New Year celebrations. I found the story fascinating because it turned something I was afraid of into something meaningful. After that conversation, I became much less nervous about firecrackers and even joined my family in the celebrations. Looking back, it was a simple conversation, but it helped me understand a traditional custom through a story told by someone I trusted.

part2.title: Describe an interesting old person you have met
part2.answer: I'd like to describe my grandfather, who is an interesting older person in my life. When I was young, he was one of the people I felt closest to, and I remember that he was good at explaining traditional things through stories. One example was the story of Nian, which he told me around Chinese New Year when I was afraid of firecrackers. Instead of simply telling me not to be scared, he explained where the custom came from and why people used fireworks to drive the monster away. What I liked most was the way he made a traditional story feel vivid and relevant to a child. He was also quite patient and never forced me to do things before I understood them. That experience made me see that older people can pass on much more than factual knowledge. They can also preserve stories, customs and values. Whenever I think about Chinese New Year now, I still associate the tradition with that conversation with my grandfather, so he remains a particularly memorable older person to me.

part2.title: Describe an impressive course/English lesson you had and enjoyed
part2.answer: I'd like to talk about a short English lesson I found online. I came across it while scrolling through short videos, and surprisingly, it was only about ten minutes long. The lesson focused on a problem that I have personally experienced as a non-native English speaker: translating everything into Chinese in my head before speaking English. The teacher explained that this makes communication slower and can easily lead to unnatural expressions. What impressed me was that the lesson gave several practical ways to change the habit. For example, I could connect objects around me directly with English words, carry vocabulary cards, and practise shadowing instead of translating sentence by sentence. The teacher also emphasized patience, because changing a language habit takes time. I found the lesson useful because it didn't just give me vocabulary; it changed the way I think about speaking English. Since then, I've tried to respond more directly in English during my IELTS practice. It was short, but it had a surprisingly lasting influence on my learning habits.

part2.title: Describe a beautiful place you have been to / a natural landscape you like
part2.answer: I'd like to describe a beautiful natural landscape I saw during my graduation trip to Yunnan. My close friend Ning and I climbed Yulong Snow Mountain in September after I finished my master's degree. When we reached an altitude of around 4,600 metres, I saw a snow-covered peak against an incredibly blue sky with moving white clouds. It was actually much more beautiful than the pictures I had seen in advertisements. I come from Chengdu, where the sky is often cloudy, so seeing such clear blue skies made the experience even more exciting for me. I remember that the clouds were moving surprisingly fast. At first, they partly covered the mountain, and then they suddenly moved away and revealed the entire peak. It felt almost like a natural performance. We took lots of photos, although none of them could fully capture what we saw with our own eyes. Looking back, that moment represents more than just a beautiful view. It was also a rewarding ending to my master's life and a memorable trip with a close friend.

part2.title: Describe an intelligent person you know
part2.answer: I'd like to describe my master's supervisor, Professor Luo, whom I consider a very intelligent person. What impressed me most was not simply his knowledge, but the way he approached complicated research problems. He could usually break a complicated question into smaller, manageable steps and guide students to think about the logic rather than just giving them an answer. Interestingly, his appearance was quite casual, which was very different from his serious attitude towards research. I remember that during my first postgraduate interview, he was wearing a slightly cartoonish T-shirt, and later I even saw him wear a wrinkled T-shirt or put it on inside out. But when it came to research, he was extremely rigorous and demanding. I learned a lot from that contrast. He made me realize that being a good researcher isn't about looking formal; it is about being curious, logical and persistent. His attitude also influenced my decision to consider pursuing a PhD, because he made research feel challenging but meaningful.

part2.title: Describe a time you used your cell phone/smart-phone to do something important
part2.answer: I'd like to talk about a time when I used my smartphone for something genuinely important. Recently, I've been preparing applications for PhD programmes overseas, so I regularly use my phone to check emails from potential supervisors. It may sound like a small thing, but during the application period, I often keep my phone nearby because I'm waiting for replies that could affect my future plans. The main issue they usually mention is funding, because international PhD tuition fees can be very high. So I need to monitor these conversations carefully and respond quickly when necessary. part2.title: Describe a place where you saw animals
part2.answer: I'd like to describe an animal experience during my graduation trip to Yunnan. One of our stops was a local zoo, which had a wider range of animals than many zoos I had visited in other cities. The most memorable part was a peacock flight show. It was the first time I'd seen this kind of performance, and there were more than thirty peacocks in the area. The funny thing was that I'm actually quite afraid of birds. I initially went because I thought it would be interesting, but when so many peacocks suddenly appeared, I became a little nervous. Some of them even came close to the audience, which made me feel even more uncomfortable. I also noticed that some parents encouraged their children to enter the performance area to take photos with the peacocks. Although I understood that they wanted their children to have fun, I felt there could be safety risks because animals can behave unpredictably. The experience was memorable because it was both exciting and slightly frightening, and it also made me think about the importance of respecting boundaries between people and animals.

I called my mother because I was frustrated and needed someone to talk to. Surprisingly, she didn't ask me to finish faster or worry about the result. Although she didn't understand the technical details of my project, her advice helped me calm down. I stopped thinking so much about when I would graduate and started concentrating on what I could actually improve. I eventually graduated three months later than I had originally expected, but I never regretted the extra time. Her advice helped me become more resilient and independent, and I still remember it when I face uncertainty.

The experience taught me to be much more careful when travelling alone. part2.title: Describe a person who encouraged you during a difficult time
part2.reference:
I'd like to describe a close friend who encouraged me while I was preparing for a postgraduate interview. At first, I didn't really like her. She quickly became close to one of my best friends, and I felt a little as if my friendship was being taken away. We also seemed completely different, and I didn't think we had much in common. I even thought some of her enthusiastic behaviour was a little fake. Later, we became deskmates, and I gradually realized that I had misunderstood her. She was genuinely friendly and outgoing. She would share snacks with me and talk about interesting things. As we spent more time together, we discovered that we actually shared quite a few interests and similar views about life. What really turned us into close friends was the way we supported each other. When I was preparing for a postgraduate interview and feeling extremely anxious, she encouraged me through many long phone calls and shared useful application information with me. Eventually, we both got into the universities we wanted. The experience taught me that first impressions can be misleading and that genuine friendship can last through different stages of life.

Stress can make a person focus only on what might go wrong. A friend who listens can help create some distance from that worry. The encouragement mattered because it came from a real relationship, rather than simply a general motivational message.

part2.title: Describe a time when a stranger helped you
part2.reference:
I'd like to describe a time when a stranger helped me during a difficult journey. I was about fifteen, and it was my first time travelling alone. On the way back from Beijing, I accidentally left my backpack at a railway station. Unfortunately, it contained my phone, cash and other important things. I didn't realize it until I had already boarded the train, so I immediately felt panicked because I had no easy way to contact my family. Luckily, I came across a kind woman who noticed that I was struggling. She helped me contact my family and even lent me some cash so that I could manage the journey. She stayed with me for much of the trip and made sure I got into the right vehicle after I got off the train. The backpack was never recovered, but I still remember her kindness. The experience taught me to be much more careful when travelling alone. It also made me realize that a small act of kindness from a stranger can make an enormous difference when someone is vulnerable.

The help mattered because I was only fifteen and away from the reassurance of familiar surroundings. It did not solve everything, and the backpack was not recovered, but it gave me a way to respond to the immediate problem. That is why I remember the woman's practical kindness so clearly.

part2.title: Describe a place where you can concentrate
part2.reference:
I'd like to describe a place where I can concentrate: a quiet café near West Lake in Hangzhou. It is on the second floor of a small building and has large windows overlooking the surroundings. I first went there when I needed somewhere peaceful to work, because I was quite busy with my master's research at the time. What I liked immediately was that it wasn't crowded or noisy. I could sit by the window, have a cup of coffee and concentrate on my work without being disturbed. Sometimes I also bring my camera and take a few photos when I need a break. The atmosphere is especially pleasant on a weekday afternoon, when the sunlight comes through the windows and the area around West Lake feels much calmer. I think I like this place because I normally spend a lot of time dealing with research and applications, so I really value somewhere that allows me to slow down. It has become one of my favourite places to recharge and focus.

The appeal is not simply the absence of noise. The light from the large windows and the possibility of sitting with a coffee make the setting comfortable enough for sustained work. I would use the space for a clear task rather than assume that moving to a café automatically improves concentration. The surroundings help, but I still need to decide what I am trying to get done.

part2.title: Describe someone who knows a lot about your local area
part2.reference:
I'd like to describe a neighbour who knows a great deal about my local area. One of my neighbours is an older person who has lived in the area for many years. What makes him interesting is that he knows a lot about local changes and traditional customs. Whenever we happen to meet, he often tells me stories about how the neighbourhood looked when he was younger. I find these conversations interesting because they are very different from what I can learn from the Internet. He also has a very practical attitude towards life and often gives simple advice rather than making complicated arguments. I don't see him every day, but our conversations are always memorable. I think people who have lived in one place for a long time can provide a different perspective on a community because they have actually experienced its changes. Talking to him has also made me more interested in the stories behind familiar places. So although we aren't close friends, I enjoy having occasional conversations with him.

I find that a local story can make an ordinary street or building feel less anonymous. It encourages me to think about who used the place before and what may have changed. His account is a starting point for that curiosity, rather than something I need to present as a verified historical lecture. The interesting part is hearing a familiar area described through another person's experience.

part2.title: Describe a film that made you laugh (comedy)
part2.reference:
I'd like to talk about a Chinese comedy called Charlotte's Troubles, also known as Goodbye Mr. Loser, starring Shen Teng and Ma Li. I watched it [when you watched it], [alone/with the people who actually watched it with you].

The main character, Xia Luo, is a frustrated middle-aged man whose career hasn't gone well. Unexpectedly, he gets a chance to go back in time while keeping his memories of the future. He uses that knowledge, especially his memories of popular songs, to become successful and win over a girl he used to have a crush on.

That process made me laugh because his apparent talent comes from knowing things that haven't happened yet. There is a ridiculous contrast between how impressive he seems to the people around him and what the audience knows about his advantage. He keeps trying to rewrite his life, and the situations he creates become increasingly absurd.

However, the film isn't only about those comic situations. Eventually, he recognises that success hasn't necessarily brought him genuine relationships or satisfaction. Some people around him don't really care about him, and he starts to appreciate the imperfect life he originally wanted to escape.

I enjoyed that combination of humour and reflection. The story made me laugh, but it also raised a question about whether external success is the same as happiness. For me, that gives the comedy more meaning than a series of jokes on their own.

part2.title: Describe an important river/lake in your country
part2.reference:
I'd like to describe West Lake, which is in Hangzhou, in eastern China. It's an urban freshwater lake, and the main lake covers roughly six square kilometres. It is much smaller than China's largest lakes. It is a broad lake rather than a river running through the city.

Its appearance is closely connected with the landscape around the water. There are tree-lined shores, causeways and views towards the surrounding hills. Different parts of the shore give visitors different perspectives, so it is not simply one viewpoint that everyone experiences in the same way. The combination of open water and greenery is what makes the setting distinctive.

My own connection is with a quiet café near West Lake. It is on the second floor and has large windows, and I have used it as a place for reading or research. That is a more specific experience I can talk about, rather than claiming that I have explored every part of the lake.

West Lake is important as a cultural landscape and a well-known destination for visitors. It also provides an outdoor setting within a large city, where the water and surrounding scenery shape the character of the area. For me, its significance is therefore both public and personal: it is a recognised feature of Hangzhou, but it is also connected with an ordinary place where I have spent time concentrating and taking a quieter break.

questions.question: What can young people learn from old people?
questions.answer: Older people have accumulated practical experience that younger people simply don't have. They can share stories about how they dealt with uncertainty, relationships and difficult decisions. At the same time, young people should not accept every traditional idea uncritically; they can compare that experience with current knowledge.

Old people have been through a lot, so their experiences can offer helpful guidance and perspective, especially during tough times. However, experience isn't a rule that must be followed without question. Circumstances may have changed, so a younger person should consider why an approach worked and whether it still fits. That allows advice to become a source of perspective rather than a substitute for independent judgement.
